followUps:
Version 4 was skipped so that nobody would confuse the new product with .NET Framework 4.x, which is still installed on millions of Windows machines.

The cross-platform line went .NET Core 1.0, 2.x, 3.0, 3.1 and then jumped to .NET 5 in November 2020. A ".NET Core 4.0" next to ".NET Framework 4.8" would have been a constant source of mistakes in documents, searches and job adverts. The jump also made the point that 5 is the successor of both lines, and the word "Core" was dropped from the name at the same time.

async and await arrived with C# 5 and .NET Framework 4.5 in 2012.

They are built on the Task type, which came one release earlier in .NET Framework 4.0 (2010) as the Task Parallel Library. So the order to remember is: tasks in 4.0, then the language keywords that make tasks easy to use in 4.5. Every modern .NET version has them, and later releases added ValueTask, async streams (IAsyncEnumerable<T>, C# 8) and await using.

No, it is not dead, but it is frozen: it still gets security and reliability fixes, and it gets no new features.

  • .NET Framework 4.8.1 is the last version. It is a part of Windows, so it is supported for as long as the Windows version it ships with.
  • Existing Web Forms, WCF and WPF apps keep running and you do not have to move them tomorrow.
  • New C# language versions, performance work, containers on Linux and new libraries only target modern .NET.

The practical rule: maintain what you have on it, start nothing new on it.

code.title: What the CLR does: bounds checks, deterministic Dispose, garbage collection

followUps:
You call unmanaged (native) code with P/Invoke: you declare the native function in C# and the runtime loads the library and converts the arguments for you.

[LibraryImport("kernel32.dll")]          // .NET 7+: marshalling code is generated at build time
private static partial uint GetCurrentProcessId();
[DllImport("libc")]                       // the older form, still works
private static extern int getpid();

Converting values between the two worlds is called marshalling. Wrap native handles in a SafeHandle so they are released even if your code forgets. On Windows you can also call COM components through COM interop.

IL (Intermediate Language) is the CPU-neutral instruction set that the C# compiler writes into your .dll; it is not machine code yet.

For example return a + b; becomes roughly ldarg.0, ldarg.1, add, ret: push two arguments on a stack, add them, return. When the method is first called, the JIT compiler in the CLR turns those instructions into real x64 or ARM64 instructions. This is why one .dll runs on Windows, Linux and macOS, and why C#, F# and VB can call each other: they all compile to the same IL. You can read it with a tool such as ILSpy.

Not in any way you can rely on: the garbage collector frees memory, and it runs when memory is short, not when you are finished with the file.

A FileStream holds an operating-system handle. If you never dispose it, the handle is closed only when a finalizer happens to run, which may be seconds or minutes later, or never before the process ends. Until then the file can stay locked and buffered data may not be written.

using (var stream = File.OpenWrite("report.csv"))
{
stream.Write(bytes, 0, bytes.Length);
}   // Dispose runs here: data flushed, handle closed

The rule: anything that implements IDisposable goes in a using.

code.title: Namespaces are names, the assembly is the file: reflection shows both

followUps:
internal means "visible only inside this assembly", and InternalsVisibleTo is an attribute that lets one named other assembly see those internal types as well.

Use internal for classes that are implementation details, so that other projects cannot depend on them and you stay free to change them. The usual reason to open the door is a test project:

// in Shop.Orders (any .cs file)
[assembly: InternalsVisibleTo("Shop.Orders.Tests")]
// or in Shop.Orders.csproj
<InternalsVisibleTo Include="Shop.Orders.Tests" />

Do not use it to share internals between production projects; if two projects need the type, it is really part of a public contract.

The manifest is the part of the assembly's metadata that describes the assembly itself: who it is and what it needs.

  • Identity: name, version, culture and, if it is signed, the public key token.
  • References: the other assemblies it depends on, with their versions.
  • Contents: the files and modules that make up the assembly, and embedded resources.
  • Exported types: type forwards to other assemblies.

For example the manifest of Shop.Orders.dll may say "version 2.1.0.0, references System.Runtime 10.0.0.0". The runtime reads it to find and load the right dependencies. ILSpy or ildasm shows it.

A transitive dependency is a package you did not ask for yourself: it comes in because a package you did ask for needs it.

Example: your project references package A 2.0. A needs B 1.3, and B needs C 4.0. You wrote one line, but B and C are restored and shipped too.

  • See them with dotnet list package --include-transitive.
  • They matter for security: a vulnerable C is your problem. dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive finds it.
  • If two packages want different versions of C, NuGet picks one by its rules, which can surprise you. Pin the version with a direct reference, or with central package management and transitive pinning.

Modern .NET is faster because performance has been a main goal of every release since .NET Core, while .NET Framework had to stay compatible and barely changed.

  • Better JIT: tiered compilation and, on by default since .NET 8, dynamic profile-guided optimisation, which re-compiles hot methods using what the program really does.
  • Fewer allocations: Span<T> and pooled buffers are used throughout the base libraries, so the garbage collector has less work.
  • New web stack: Kestrel and the ASP.NET Core pipeline replaced System.Web and IIS-bound code.
  • Hardware instructions: string search, JSON and LINQ use vector (SIMD) instructions.

An upgrade with no code change often cuts CPU use noticeably; measure it for your own service.

I would keep the WCF service working first and decide per service whether to keep SOAP or replace it, because WCF server hosting does not exist in modern .NET.

  • Callers of WCF: the WCF client packages (System.ServiceModel.*) run on modern .NET, so a migrated app can still call an old service.
  • Keep the SOAP contract: move the service to CoreWCF, the supported port of the server side. Clients do not change.
  • Change the contract: rewrite as gRPC (internal, service to service) or a REST API (public), when you control all the clients.
  • Leave it: keep it on .NET Framework behind the proxy until its turn comes.

Yes. They are separate installations and do not interfere with each other.

.NET Framework is one copy that is part of Windows. Modern .NET installs each version in its own folder (dotnet/shared/Microsoft.NETCore.App/8.0.x, 10.0.x and so on), or travels inside the app when you publish self-contained. So one Windows server can run a .NET Framework 4.8 site, a .NET 8 API and a .NET 10 API at once.

On IIS give each ASP.NET Core app its own application pool set to "No Managed Code"; the ASP.NET Core Module starts the right runtime. This is what makes a step-by-step migration possible: old and new run next to each other behind one address.

You do. A self-contained app carries its own copy of the runtime, so a runtime security fix only reaches it when you build and deploy the app again.

Compare the two:

  • Framework-dependent: the app uses the runtime installed on the machine or in the base container image. Operations patch the machine or you rebuild on the new base image, and every app on it is fixed.
  • Self-contained: the runtime version is fixed at publish time. Updating the server changes nothing for that app.

So self-contained needs a pipeline that rebuilds on every monthly .NET patch, with the SDK kept up to date. Forgetting this is how apps end up running a runtime with known vulnerabilities.

A runtime identifier (RID) is a short name for the operating system and CPU that a build is meant for, such as win-x64, linux-x64, linux-arm64 or osx-arm64.

IL is portable, but the runtime itself and any native libraries are not, so the SDK must know the target when it has to include them:

dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 --self-contained

You need a RID for self-contained, single-file, ReadyToRun and Native AOT publishing. A framework-dependent app without a RID is portable: the same output runs wherever the matching runtime is installed. Use the portable RIDs above, not distribution-specific ones.

Trimming removes code that the build cannot see being used, so it breaks anything that finds code at run time by name instead of by a normal reference.

  • Reflection: Type.GetType("Shop.Order"), reading properties by name, Activator.CreateInstance.
  • Reflection-based serializers and mappers, including System.Text.Json without source generation.
  • Assembly scanning ("register every class that implements IHandler") and plugins loaded from disk.

The failure is nasty because it appears at run time, as a missing member or an empty JSON object. Fix it by treating trim warnings (such as IL2026) as errors, using source generators, and testing the published, trimmed output and not only the debug build.

I would treat it as a planned upgrade to .NET 10, the current LTS, done service by service, because .NET 8 support ends on 10 November 2026 and after that it gets no security fixes.

  1. Inventory: list every service with its target framework and owner.
  2. Pilot: upgrade one low-risk service: change TargetFramework to net10.0, update packages and the base image, read the breaking-changes list, run the tests.
  3. Roll out: repeat in batches with a canary or slot deployment and watch error rate and latency.
  4. Prevent a repeat: a CI check that fails builds targeting an unsupported version, and a yearly upgrade slot in the plan.

LTS to LTS is usually a small change per service; the work is in the number of services.

I would choose an STS release when it has a feature or a performance gain the product needs now, and the team already upgrades every year.

STS releases are not betas. They get the same testing and the same monthly patches as LTS; only the support period is shorter (24 months). The cost is that you must move to the next version inside that period.

  • Good fit: services you deploy continuously in containers, where an upgrade is a one-line change plus a test run.
  • Poor fit: software installed at customers, or systems with a slow release and validation cycle. Stay on LTS there.

A servicing update is a patch release, for example 10.0.1 to 10.0.2, that contains security and reliability fixes and no new features or deliberate breaking changes. They normally come out monthly, on the second Tuesday.

How it reaches a server depends on how you deploy:

  • Machine runtime: update it with the package manager on Linux, or Microsoft Update or an installer on Windows. A framework-dependent app picks up the newest installed patch of its major version by itself.
  • Containers: rebuild the image on the refreshed base image and redeploy.
  • Managed platforms such as Azure App Service patch the runtime for you.
  • Self-contained apps: rebuild with the updated SDK and redeploy.

code.title: IL in the dll, the JIT at first call, and which runtime and BCL you run on

followUps:
Tiered compilation means the JIT compiles each method quickly and roughly first, and compiles it again with full optimisation only if the method turns out to be used a lot.

  • Tier 0: fast to produce, slow to run. Good for start-up, because most methods run once or twice.
  • Tier 1: after a method has been called about 30 times, a background thread re-compiles it with optimisations and swaps it in.

Since .NET 8, dynamic PGO is on by default: tier 0 code also records what really happens (which types appear, which branches are taken) and tier 1 uses that. The effect to know: the first requests after a deployment are slower than later ones, which is why you warm up an instance before it takes traffic.

The SDK version is the set of tools that builds your code; the target framework is the version of .NET your app is built for and runs on. They do not have to match.

SDK versionTarget framework
Whatcompiler, dotnet CLI, MSBuildthe API set and runtime
Wherebuild machine; pinned in global.json<TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework> in the project
Example10.0.100net8.0

A newer SDK can build older targets, so the .NET 10 SDK builds a net8.0 project. The server needs only the runtime for the target framework, never the SDK.

Native AOT removes the JIT and the IL from the running app: everything is compiled to machine code at build time into one native executable.

  • Gone: JIT compilation at run time, tiered compilation, loading new assemblies, generating code on the fly (Reflection.Emit), and unrestricted reflection.
  • Still there: the garbage collector, the type system and the base libraries your code uses, linked into the executable in trimmed form.

You gain start-up in milliseconds, lower memory and no runtime to install. You pay with a build per operating system and CPU, and libraries that depend on reflection must be replaced by ones that use source generators.

code.title: One source file, two targets: version-specific code with #if

followUps:
Multi-targeting means one project is compiled several times, once per target framework, and the NuGet package then contains one .dll for each.

<TargetFrameworks>net10.0;netstandard2.0</TargetFrameworks>

For code that differs, use the symbols the SDK defines for each target:

#if NET8_0_OR_GREATER
return Math.Clamp(value, min, max);
#else
return value < min ? min : value > max ? max : value;
#endif

You can also include whole files or package references per target with a Condition in the project file. Keep the #if blocks few and small, and run the tests against every target.

Because .NET Standard 2.1 includes features that need changes inside the runtime itself, and Microsoft decided not to make those changes in .NET Framework.

Examples are full runtime support for Span<T> and default interface methods. .NET Framework is a component of Windows used by a huge amount of old software, so changing its runtime carries a high compatibility risk. Version 4.8 therefore stops at .NET Standard 2.0.

The consequence for a library author: target netstandard2.0 if .NET Framework apps must be able to use the library, and add a modern target next to it if you want the newer APIs.

Because a source generator is loaded into the C# compiler, and the compiler runs in more than one runtime.

On the command line (dotnet build) the compiler runs on modern .NET. Inside Visual Studio it runs on .NET Framework. A generator has to load in both, and the only target that both can load is netstandard2.0. The same rule applies to Roslyn analyzers.

This limits only the generator's own code. The code it generates is compiled into your project and can use any feature your project's target framework allows.

code.title: TimeProvider (.NET 8): testing time-dependent code with a fake clock

followUps:
HybridCache solves two things that IMemoryCache leaves to you: sharing the cache between servers, and stopping many requests from rebuilding the same entry at once.

  • Two levels in one call: a fast in-memory copy on each instance, backed by a distributed cache such as Redis. IMemoryCache is per instance only, so five instances hold five separate caches.
  • Stampede protection: if 200 requests miss the same key together, the factory runs once and the others wait for its result. With IMemoryCache all 200 may hit the database.
  • Serialization and tags: it serializes values for the second level, and you can evict a group of entries by tag.
var product = await cache.GetOrCreateAsync($"product:{id}",
async ct => await db.Products.FindAsync([id], ct));

Because from .NET 9 ASP.NET Core can produce the OpenAPI document itself, so the template no longer needs a third-party package for it.

Swashbuckle is a community project, and at the time it had gone a long period without the maintenance needed to keep up with new .NET releases. Microsoft added the Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi package instead:

builder.Services.AddOpenApi();
app.MapOpenApi();          // serves /openapi/v1.json

What changed for you: the built-in package produces the JSON document only, with no web page. If you want the interactive page, add a UI such as Swagger UI or Scalar and point it at that document. Swashbuckle still works if you add it yourself.

TimeProvider is a built-in "clock" abstraction (.NET 8) that you inject so that tests can control the time instead of reading the real clock.

Code that calls DateTime.UtcNow directly cannot be tested for "the token expires after 60 minutes" without waiting 60 minutes. With an injected clock the test moves time forward itself:

public class TokenService(TimeProvider clock)
{
public bool IsExpired(Token t) => clock.GetUtcNow() > t.ExpiresAt;
}
// production: services.AddSingleton(TimeProvider.System);
// test:       var clock = new FakeTimeProvider(); clock.Advance(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(61));

It also creates timers and delays, so retry and timeout code becomes testable. FakeTimeProvider comes from the Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing package.

The simplest way is to let the old app stay the owner of login and let the new app ask it who the user is, so the user signs in once.

  • System.Web adapters: Microsoft's migration library (Microsoft.AspNetCore.SystemWebAdapters) has remote authentication and remote session: the ASP.NET Core app forwards the request's cookies to an endpoint in the old app and receives the user and session values.
  • Shared cookie: configure both apps to read the same authentication cookie, with the same key ring and cookie name, on the same domain.
  • Best end state: move both to one identity provider with OpenID Connect, for example Microsoft Entra ID. Each app validates the same sign-in on its own.

Put both apps behind one host name with a reverse proxy (YARP) so the cookie is sent to both.

Web Forms cannot be ported, because modern .NET has no Web Forms at all, so each page is either left where it is or rewritten.

  1. Leave them running on .NET Framework behind the proxy. Nothing forces a rewrite on day one.
  2. Move the logic out of the code-behind files into class libraries that target netstandard2.0, so old and new can both call it. This is the most valuable step.
  3. Rewrite page by page, most-used or most-changed first, as Razor Pages or Blazor (closest to the component model), or as a React or Angular front end over an API.
  4. Retire pages nobody uses; check the access logs first.

The proxy routes each URL to whichever app owns it today.

I would present it as reducing risk and cost in numbers the business cares about, not as "the technology is old".

  • Risk: which parts are out of support and what a security incident or a failed audit would cost.
  • Running cost: modern .NET usually needs less CPU and runs on Linux containers; estimate the saving from a measured pilot, not from a blog post.
  • Delivery speed: how long changes take in the old code today, with real examples from the last quarter.
  • People: hiring and keeping developers for Web Forms and WCF gets harder every year.

Then ask for a small first step with a visible result, for example one service migrated in six weeks, and report measured numbers before asking for the next step. An incremental plan is much easier to approve than a rewrite.

Startup.cs was a class with ConfigureServices and Configure methods that the old generic host called to register services and build the pipeline. It went away because two methods and a class were extra ceremony.

From .NET 6 the same two jobs sit in one top-level Program.cs: services are added on builder.Services, the pipeline on app. Fewer files and less to explain to a newcomer; the behaviour is the same. Old projects with a Startup class still run, and you can migrate by moving the two methods' bodies into Program.cs.

The generic host (Host.CreateApplicationBuilder) gives any program the same configuration, logging, DI and lifetime as a web app, without the web server.

Use it for worker services that read a queue, scheduled jobs, and console tools that want the usual appsettings.json and ILogger. You add BackgroundService classes and the host starts them and stops them on Ctrl+C or SIGTERM.

var builder = Host.CreateApplicationBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddHostedService<QueueWorker>();
await builder.Build().RunAsync();

On SIGTERM or Ctrl+C the host stops accepting new work, tells hosted services to stop, and waits for running requests to finish up to a time limit.

  1. The application lifetime fires ApplicationStopping.
  2. Kestrel stops listening and lets in-flight requests complete.
  3. Each IHostedService.StopAsync runs; the CancellationToken of a BackgroundService is cancelled.
  4. Disposable services are disposed.

The limit is HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout, 30 seconds by default since .NET 8. If your orchestrator kills the container sooner (Kubernetes default 30 seconds), work is cut off, so keep long jobs checking their token.

code.title: Dependency injection by hand: swap the dependency without touching the class

followUps:
Dependency inversion is a design rule; dependency injection is one technique to follow it.

Inversion (the D in SOLID) says high-level code should depend on an abstraction, not on a concrete low-level class. OrderService depends on IEmailSender, and the SMTP class also depends on that interface, so the arrow of dependency is reversed. Injection is how the object gets the implementation: someone passes it in, usually through the constructor. You can do injection without inversion (injecting a concrete class), and a DI container is only a tool that automates the passing.

The service locator is code that asks a global container for its dependencies, for example provider.GetRequiredService<IEmailSender>() inside a method, instead of receiving them in the constructor.

It is an anti-pattern because the dependencies become invisible: the constructor says nothing, so you only learn what a class needs by reading its body or from a run-time exception. Tests have to build a container. Lifetimes are easy to get wrong.

Acceptable places are narrow: framework glue such as a factory that must create scoped services on demand (use IServiceScopeFactory) or a plug-in lookup. Normal business classes should use constructor injection.

You use a third-party container when the built-in one lacks a feature you really need. Otherwise stay with the built-in one.

The built-in container handles constructor injection, three lifetimes, keyed services and open generics. Typical gaps are: decorators registered in one line, assembly scanning by convention, property injection, child containers and module-style registration (Autofac, Scrutor for scanning and decoration, Lamar).

The cost: another dependency, another set of rules, and behaviour that differs from the framework's. If one extension method that registers a decorator by hand solves the problem, I would write that and not add a container.

code.title: A request pipeline built from delegates: order changes the result

followUps:
Authorization would run without a known user, so every protected endpoint would answer 401 or 403 even for a user who sent a valid token.

UseAuthentication reads the cookie or token and sets HttpContext.User. UseAuthorization then checks that user against the endpoint's policy. If the order is swapped, the user is still anonymous when the policy is checked, so [Authorize] endpoints fail for everyone. The error is easy to miss in the browser because it looks like a wrong permission; the fix is only to swap the two lines. Both must also come after UseRouting (added automatically) so that the endpoint is known.

Short-circuiting means a middleware writes the response itself and does not call next, so the later parts of the pipeline never run.

app.Use(async (ctx, next) =>
{
if (!ctx.Request.Headers.ContainsKey("X-Api-Key"))
{
ctx.Response.StatusCode = 401;   // answer here
return;                          // no call to next()
}
await next();
});

Static files, CORS preflight, authentication failures and health checks do this. The response still travels back out through the middleware that came earlier, so a logging middleware at the top still sees the 401.

UseCors goes after UseRouting and before UseAuthentication and UseAuthorization.

The reason is the browser's preflight request: an OPTIONS request that carries no credentials. If authentication or authorization ran first, the preflight would be rejected with 401, the browser would never send the real request, and the page would show a CORS error even though the real cause is auth. CORS must also run before any middleware that can short-circuit, such as response caching, or the CORS headers are missing from those responses. With WebApplication the routing step is added for you, so in practice you write app.UseCors() first, then the two auth lines.

code.title: Writing a middleware: timing, a header and a short circuit

followUps:
Because a middleware class is created once for the whole application, so a scoped service passed to its constructor would live forever and be shared by all requests.

That is the captive dependency problem. A scoped DbContext held by the middleware would be used by many requests at the same time, and it is not thread-safe. InvokeAsync runs once per request, and the framework resolves its extra parameters from the request scope, so each request gets its own instance.

public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext ctx, AppDbContext db) { ... }

With the validation on in development the app even throws at start-up when you get this wrong.

Use adds a middleware that can call the next one; Run adds a final one that ends the pipeline and has no next.

app.Use(async (ctx, next) => { /* before */ await next(); /* after */ });
app.Run(async ctx => await ctx.Response.WriteAsync("end of the line"));

Anything added after a Run never executes. Modern apps rarely call Run, because endpoints (MapGet, MapControllers) are the normal terminal part. There is also Map, which branches the pipeline for a path prefix such as /health.

Write a filter when the logic needs to know about the MVC action: which action runs, its arguments, the model state or the result object.

Middleware sees only raw HTTP and runs for every request, including static files and endpoints that are not controllers. A filter runs only around controller actions (or minimal API endpoints with endpoint filters) and can read arguments such as the validated model, return an IActionResult directly, or wrap the action result.

Examples: logging, correlation ids, CORS and exception handling are middleware. Validating the model, checking that the order belongs to the caller, caching an action result are filters.

code.title: Choosing the environment name, with Production as the safe default

followUps:
Because you want to test the exact bytes that you will run in production, and a different build for each environment would mean the tested thing is not the shipped thing.

Build once in CI, produce one container image or package, and promote it through dev, test and production. Everything that differs lives outside the artifact: environment variables, a vault, the platform's app settings. If you rebuild per environment, a different package version or compiler setting can slip in, and "it worked in staging" no longer proves anything. It also makes rollback simple: redeploy the previous artifact.

Production secrets come from a secret store that the platform provides at run time, never from files in the repository.

  • Azure Key Vault, read by the app with a managed identity so there is no password to store. Add it as a configuration source or use Key Vault references in App Service.
  • Environment variables or mounted secrets set by the orchestrator (Kubernetes secrets, container app secrets).

User secrets (dotnet user-secrets) exist only for local development and are not encrypted. A secret that was ever committed must be treated as leaked and rotated.

launchSettings.json is a file in the Properties folder that sets up how dotnet run and Visual Studio start the app on your machine: URLs, ports and environment variables such as ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development.

It holds named profiles (for example "http", "https", "IIS Express"). It is only for local development: it is not part of dotnet publish output, and the server never reads it. Do not put secrets in it, as it is normally committed. In production the same settings come from the host: environment variables or the app's configuration in the portal.

code.title: Layered configuration: later source wins, bound to a typed class

followUps:
For a singleton that must see changes you inject IOptionsMonitor<T>.

InterfaceLifetimeSees changes?
IOptions<T>singletonno, read once
IOptionsSnapshot<T>scopedyes, per request
IOptionsMonitor<T>singletonyes, live, with OnChange

IOptionsSnapshot is scoped, so it cannot go into a singleton. Read monitor.CurrentValue at the moment you need the value and do not copy it into a field in the constructor, or you lose the updates.

You use a double underscore in place of the colon: Smtp:Host becomes Smtp__Host.

Colons are not allowed in environment variable names on some systems, so the configuration system treats __ as the section separator. Arrays use the index: Cors__Origins__0=https://a.example and Cors__Origins__1=https://b.example. Names are not case-sensitive in the configuration system. In Kubernetes or a container app you set exactly these names in the deployment settings.

Validating on start makes a wrong setting stop the deployment immediately, not fail on some request at 3 a.m.

Without it, a missing connection string or a port of 0 only shows when the code first uses it, maybe hours after release. With validation the app refuses to start, and the platform keeps the old version running.

builder.Services.AddOptions<SmtpOptions>()
.BindConfiguration("Smtp")
.ValidateDataAnnotations()   // [Required], [Range(1, 65535)]
.ValidateOnStart();

Without ValidateOnStart the check runs only the first time the options are read.

code.title: Lifetimes in a tiny container, and a captive dependency

followUps:
Because a DbContext is not thread-safe and keeps a change tracker, so it must be shared inside one request and never between requests.

Scoped gives you one instance per HTTP request: the repository and the service you call in that request see the same tracked entities and the same unit of work, and SaveChanges saves everything together. A singleton would be used by many requests at once and would grow forever; a transient would give each class its own context, so changes could not be saved in one transaction. In background code, create your own scope or use IDbContextFactory.

They are not disposed when you expect: the root container keeps a reference to them until the application shuts down, so they pile up as a memory leak.

The container disposes the IDisposable objects it created when their scope ends. For a service resolved from the root provider there is no short scope, only the app's lifetime. In a long-running worker that resolves a transient disposable from the root provider every minute, memory and handles grow. The fix is to create a scope (using var scope = provider.CreateScope()) for each unit of work and resolve from scope.ServiceProvider.

They used a factory delegate, a custom factory class or a small lookup of implementations, because the default container could not tell two registrations of one interface apart.

services.AddSingleton<PdfExporter>();
services.AddSingleton<CsvExporter>();
services.AddSingleton<Func<string, IExporter>>(sp => key => key switch
{
"pdf" => sp.GetRequiredService<PdfExporter>(),
_     => sp.GetRequiredService<CsvExporter>()
});

Since .NET 8, AddKeyedSingleton<IExporter, PdfExporter>("pdf") and [FromKeyedServices("pdf")] do this directly.

Group endpoints by feature and give each group its own file with an extension method, so Program.cs stays a short list.

// Orders/OrderEndpoints.cs
public static class OrderEndpoints
{
public static IEndpointRouteBuilder MapOrders(this IEndpointRouteBuilder app)
{
var g = app.MapGroup("/api/orders").RequireAuthorization();
g.MapGet("/{id:int}", GetById);
g.MapPost("/", Create);
return app;
}
}
// Program.cs:  app.MapOrders().MapCustomers();

Use MapGroup for shared prefix, auth and filters, put handlers in static methods and keep logic in services. If the team prefers conventions, controllers are the other good answer at that size.

[ApiController] turns on API-specific conventions so that you write less repeated code in each action.

  • Automatic 400: if the model is invalid, the action is not called and a ValidationProblemDetails response is returned.
  • Binding inference: complex types come from the body, simple ones from route or query, services from DI.
  • Attribute routing is required, and error status codes produce Problem Details.

Without it you write if (!ModelState.IsValid) return BadRequest(ModelState); in every action. Put it on a base controller or on the assembly.

TypedResults are helpers that return a concrete result type such as Ok<Order> or NotFound, so the compiler and OpenAPI know exactly what the endpoint can return.

app.MapGet("/orders/{id}", async Task<Results<Ok<Order>, NotFound>> (int id, IOrderService s) =>
await s.Find(id) is { } o ? TypedResults.Ok(o) : TypedResults.NotFound());

With plain Results.Ok(o) the return type is IResult, so the documentation must be added by hand with attributes. Typed results also make unit tests simple, because you can check the type of the returned object without running HTTP.

code.title: Model validation at the edge returns every error at once

followUps:
Filters run in a fixed order, from the outside in: authorization, resource, action (and model binding between them), then exception and result filters on the way out.

  1. Authorization filters decide whether the caller may continue.
  2. Resource filters run before model binding, good for caching.
  3. Action filters run just before and after the action method, with the bound arguments.
  4. Exception filters handle exceptions thrown by the action.
  5. Result filters run around the execution of the result (the JSON written).

On the way out the order reverses. Filters of the same type run global first, then controller, then action.

Not by default: the request body is a forward-only stream, so after one component reads it, the next one finds it empty.

If a middleware must look at the body (for example to log it), call Request.EnableBuffering() first, read it, then set Request.Body.Position = 0 so that model binding can read it again. It costs memory for large bodies, so limit it to the routes that need it. A better design is to log the bound object in a filter, after binding, instead of the raw stream.

Business rules belong in the domain or application layer, not in the controller or in annotations, because the same rule must hold no matter who calls the code.

The API edge checks shape: is the field present, is it a number, is the length sensible. The domain checks meaning: an order cannot be shipped before it is paid, a discount cannot exceed 30 percent, stock must be available. If the rule sits only in the controller, a background job or a second API that creates orders skips it. The domain throws a clear exception or returns a result, and the API turns that into a 400 or 409.

code.title: Turning exceptions into one Problem Details shape

followUps:
Mostly no: a missing order is a normal outcome, not an exceptional one, so return a result and keep exceptions for real faults.

Exceptions are slow when thrown often (stack capture costs microseconds each) and they hide the possible outcomes from the method signature. A lookup can return null or a small result type, and the endpoint turns it into 404:

var order = await repo.FindAsync(id, ct);
return order is null ? Results.NotFound() : Results.Ok(order);

Exceptions suit things nobody planned for: database down, null bug, broken invariant.

Validation errors are a Problem Details object with an extra errors field that maps each property name to a list of messages. The type is ValidationProblemDetails.

{ "type": "https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc9110#section-15.5.1",
"title": "One or more validation errors occurred.",
"status": 400,
"errors": { "Quantity": ["must be between 1 and 100"] } }

A client can show each message beside its field. [ApiController] returns this shape automatically; in minimal APIs return Results.ValidationProblem(errors). Keeping every error in one format means the front end needs one error parser.

Put a trace identifier in the Problem Details body and write the same identifier in every log line for that request.

ASP.NET Core adds traceId to Problem Details responses already; it comes from Activity.Current (the W3C trace id). The client reports "error, trace 4bf92f35…", and you search the log store or Application Insights for it and see the whole request, including the stack trace that was hidden from the client. With OpenTelemetry the same id also links the calls to other services, so one search shows the full chain.

Because the string is built before the logger knows whether the message will be used, and because it destroys the structure that makes logs searchable.

log.LogInformation($"Order {id} for {user}");        // bad
log.LogInformation("Order {OrderId} for {User}", id, user);  // good

With interpolation the text is formatted and allocated even if Information is switched off, and every message becomes a different string, so you cannot group or filter by OrderId. With a template the provider stores OrderId=42 as a field, and you can query it. The CA2254 analyzer flags this mistake.

A log scope adds shared values to every log line written inside a block, so you do not repeat them in each message.

using (log.BeginScope(new Dictionary<string, object> { ["OrderId"] = 42, ["CorrelationId"] = cid }))
{
log.LogInformation("Reserving stock");
log.LogInformation("Charging card");   // both lines carry OrderId and CorrelationId
}

ASP.NET Core already opens a scope for each request with the trace id and request path. Scopes need to be enabled in the provider's options (for console, IncludeScopes), and structured providers such as Application Insights store them as fields.

Put the level in configuration that can change while the app runs, and use the platform's setting, not a new build.

Levels are read from Logging:LogLevel, so an environment variable such as Logging__LogLevel__Default=Debug or Logging__LogLevel__Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore=Information sets them. In App Service or a container app you change the setting and the app restarts with it. With a file-based source and reload-on-change the level changes with no restart. Turn it back afterwards: debug logs cost money and can contain personal data.

code.title: The browser's CORS decision, modelled as a check on origin and method

followUps:
Because CORS is enforced by the browser, not by the server; Postman and server code do not check it at all.

The API receives the request and answers it. The browser looks at the response headers and, if there is no Access-Control-Allow-Origin that allows the page's origin, it hides the response from your JavaScript and writes a CORS error in the console. So CORS protects the user's browser; it is not an access-control feature for your API. Anyone can call the API with a script or curl, so you still need authentication.

A preflight is an automatic OPTIONS request that the browser sends first, asking "may I send this request?", before it sends a request that is not "simple".

It happens for methods like PUT and DELETE, for JSON bodies (Content-Type: application/json) and for custom headers such as Authorization. The browser sends Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers; the API answers with the allowed ones, and the browser caches that answer for Access-Control-Max-Age seconds. A plain GET or a form POST skips it. A slow preflight adds a round trip, so set a max age.

Because the combination would let any website on the internet make logged-in requests as the user and read the answer, so the rules forbid it.

With credentials (cookies, client certificates) the response must name one exact origin; the wildcard * is not accepted by the browser, and ASP.NET Core throws at start-up for AllowAnyOrigin() together with AllowCredentials(). Instead list the origins: WithOrigins("https://shop.example.com").AllowCredentials(). If you use bearer tokens in the Authorization header and no cookies, credentials mode is not needed, but you should still name your origins.

code.title: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter

followUps:
Socket exhaustion means the machine runs out of free network ports, so new outgoing connections fail with errors like "address already in use".

Disposing a HttpClient closes the object but the operating system keeps the closed TCP socket in a TIME_WAIT state for about 4 minutes. A service that creates a new client for each call, at 200 calls a second, piles up tens of thousands of sockets and hits the limit. The symptoms are SocketException under load that disappears when load stops. Reusing clients through IHttpClientFactory shares the pooled connections.

A retry keeps asking a failing service; a circuit breaker stops asking for a while, so the service can recover and your threads are not wasted.

After a number of failures the breaker "opens" and calls fail instantly, with no network call, for a period such as 30 seconds. Then it lets one trial call through ("half-open"); if that works it closes. Retries alone make an overloaded service worse, because every client sends more traffic. In .NET use AddStandardResilienceHandler() (Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience, built on Polly), which includes retry, circuit breaker and timeouts.

Jitter adds a random amount to each wait so that many clients do not all retry at the same moment.

Suppose 1,000 clients lose the connection at the same second and all wait exactly 2 seconds. At second 2 they all hit the recovering server together, and it falls over again, then again at 4 seconds. With a random wait between, say, 1.5 and 2.5 seconds the load spreads over a full second. Exponential backoff reduces how often each client tries, and jitter spreads the clients apart; you need both.

code.title: A background worker that stops cleanly on cancellation

followUps:
You need a lock that only one instance can hold, or you move the schedule out of the app.

  • Distributed lock: at each tick every instance tries to take a lease, for example a row in the database with an expiry, a Redis lock or an Azure Blob lease. Only the winner runs the job.
  • One trigger: a timer-triggered Azure Function or a Kubernetes CronJob runs once by design.
  • Job library: Hangfire or Quartz with a shared store coordinates instances.

Make the job idempotent as well, because a lease can expire during a slow run and a second instance may start.

A dead-letter queue is a side queue where messages go after they failed too many times, so one bad message does not block the others.

A queue such as Azure Service Bus delivers a message; if the handler throws, the message comes back and is tried again. After the maximum delivery count (default 10) it is moved to the dead-letter queue with the reason. People then inspect it, fix the cause (bad data, a bug) and resubmit it. You should alert on the dead-letter count: a growing one means work is being lost quietly.

The host cancels its token and waits for it to finish within the shutdown timeout; after that the process is killed, and any unfinished work is lost.

So the worker must watch the stoppingToken, finish or hand back the current item, and not start new items. For queue work, do not complete a message until it has been handled; an unfinished message simply reappears for another instance. Keep long jobs in small steps that can resume, and make them idempotent. In Kubernetes also set terminationGracePeriodSeconds to be at least as long as ShutdownTimeout.

Cold start is the delay while a new instance starts, and you reduce it by making that instance smaller, warmer or always present.

  • Plan: Premium or Flex Consumption plans keep instances pre-warmed or always ready; the basic Consumption plan can scale to zero.
  • Package: deploy with "run from package", avoid huge dependencies, and trim start-up work. ReadyToRun compilation reduces JIT time.
  • Code: do no slow work in Program.cs; create HttpClient through the factory; load heavy data lazily.

If the function is called every few minutes, a timer ping is a poor substitute for the right plan.

A function key only says "this caller knows a shared secret"; real authentication says who the caller is.

A key is sent in a header or query string, cannot be limited to one user, is easy to leak, and rotating it breaks all callers. With Microsoft Entra ID (App Service authentication, or JWT validation in code) you get a verified identity, claims and roles, tokens that expire, and an audit trail. Keys are fine for a quick webhook from a trusted system, or on top of other protection; for anything with user data use Entra ID or another real identity provider.

You change the project to a console-style app with its own Program.cs and replace the in-process types with the isolated ones. The in-process model support ends in November 2026, so it is a one-way move.

  • Packages: Microsoft.Azure.Functions.Worker and the matching extension packages replace Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Functions.
  • Attributes and bindings come from the Worker.Extensions.* packages.
  • Start-up and DI move to Program.cs; middleware is now possible.
  • The function return values become output binding types; ILogger comes from DI.

Test locally with Core Tools, and check Durable Functions code, which needs its isolated packages.

code.title: An end-to-end test of a pipeline, with the dependency replaced by a fake

followUps:
Because the in-memory provider is not a relational database, so tests pass that would fail on SQL Server, and the reverse.

It does not enforce foreign keys, unique indexes or transactions the same way, does not translate your LINQ to SQL (so a query that cannot run on the real database passes), and has no real concurrency checks. Use a real database in a container (Testcontainers with SQL Server or PostgreSQL) for integration tests. SQLite in-memory is a lighter option, but its SQL dialect still differs, so run the main paths on the real engine.

Register a fake authentication scheme in the test host that always signs in a user you define, and send requests with that scheme.

builder.ConfigureTestServices(s =>
s.AddAuthentication("Test")
.AddScheme<AuthenticationSchemeOptions, TestAuthHandler>("Test", _ => { }));
client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Authorization = new("Test");

The TestAuthHandler returns a ticket with the claims you want, for example the role Admin. You test the real authorization rules without needing a real identity provider. Make a second client with no claims to test the 403 case.

Give every test its own clean data, and share only the expensive parts such as the started app and the database container.

  • Start the container and the factory once per test class or collection (IClassFixture).
  • Reset between tests with a respawn tool such as Respawn, or wrap each test in a transaction that is rolled back.
  • Create the data each test needs inside that test, with unique ids, so tests do not depend on order and can run in parallel.

Slow tests are usually caused by starting a new host or database per test.

I would pick a case where the pattern had become more code than the problem, and say what I learned.

A good example: a team wrapped EF Core in a generic repository and unit of work "for flexibility". Years later there was never a second database, but every new query needed a new repository method, and tests only mocked what the repository returned. We removed the layer and used DbContext directly in the handlers, with a few well-named query classes. The code shrank, and queries became easier to optimise. The lesson I give is: add a pattern when you can name today's pain, not a pain you might have.

The most misused one is the repository (and generic repository) on top of EF Core, followed by the singleton as a global variable.

The repository is added by habit to "hide the database", but EF Core already is that abstraction, and the wrapper then blocks projections, includes and tracking control. The static singleton becomes hidden shared state that makes tests depend on each other. Another is inheritance used for reuse, where composition would be simpler. In reviews I ask: what changes independently here, and what would the code look like without the pattern?

I teach them through real code and small exercises, not through a list of names.

  • In code reviews, name the pattern when it fits, and explain the problem it solves.
  • Walk through the framework's own examples: middleware is chain of responsibility, IHttpClientFactory is a factory, Stream wrappers are decorators.
  • Ask juniors to refactor a small piece of messy code (a long switch into a strategy) and compare before and after.

I also tell them the warning signs: a class named Manager or Helper, and interfaces with one implementation that never changes.

code.title: Thread-safe lazy singleton with Lazy<T>, and a factory that hides the choice

followUps:
Because the class that uses it reaches out to a global instance, so a test cannot replace it, and state left in it by one test leaks into the next.

A static Config.Instance.Timeout inside a method cannot be swapped for a fake, and the constructor does not show the dependency. Tests that run in parallel share the one object. The fix keeps "one instance" but moves the control to the container: AddSingleton<IConfigService, ConfigService>() and constructor injection. The class is still a singleton in lifetime, but tests pass their own instance.

Use Lazy<T>, which does the locking for you, or a static field initialised by the runtime.

private static readonly Lazy<Cache> _inst = new(() => new Cache());
public static Cache Instance => _inst.Value;

The classic hand-written version needs double-checked locking with a volatile field, and it is easy to get wrong. A static readonly field (static readonly Cache I = new();) is also safe, because the runtime runs the static initialiser once, but it is created when the type is first touched, not exactly when first needed. In a DI app, prefer AddSingleton and avoid hand-made ones.

Factory method creates one product through an overridable method; abstract factory creates a whole family of related products.

Factory method example: a base class has CreateParser() and a subclass returns a CsvParser. Abstract factory example: an IUiFactory with CreateButton() and CreateMenu(), where the dark theme factory gives dark versions of both and they always match. In modern C# you often replace both with a simple function or a DI registration that picks the type, so use the full patterns only when families of objects must vary together.

code.title: Decorator: caching added around a repository without changing it

followUps:
A decorator adds behaviour to an object, and a proxy controls access to it; the code often looks the same, but the purpose differs.

Decorator: the caller chooses to stack extras, such as logging, caching or compression (GZipStream around a stream). Proxy: it stands in for the real object and decides whether, when and how to reach it: lazy loading (EF Core lazy-loading proxies), a remote proxy for a web service, a permission check before the call. If the wrapper adds a feature, call it a decorator; if it guards or hides the real object, call it a proxy.

The built-in container has no decorator feature, so you either write a registration by hand or use the Scrutor library.

services.AddSingleton<SqlOrderRepo>();
services.AddSingleton<IOrderRepo>(sp =>
new LoggingOrderRepo(sp.GetRequiredService<SqlOrderRepo>(),
sp.GetRequiredService<ILogger<LoggingOrderRepo>>()));
// With Scrutor:
services.AddSingleton<IOrderRepo, SqlOrderRepo>();
services.Decorate<IOrderRepo, LoggingOrderRepo>();

Register the concrete inner class itself so it is not mistaken for the interface.

A facade becomes a god class when it stops being a thin entry point and starts holding the logic itself.

Signs: it has dozens of methods for unrelated tasks, every other class depends on it, it needs ten constructor parameters, and every change touches it. A healthy facade only calls the subsystems in the right order (PlaceOrder calls stock, payment and mail). When business rules start to appear in the facade, move them into the domain, or split it by use case into several smaller facades.

code.title: Strategy and Observer together: swappable rules and a notification list

followUps:
Both swap behaviour behind an interface, but Strategy is chosen from outside and stays, while State changes itself as the object moves through its life.

Strategy: a checkout gets a TenPercent or FlatFive rule from the caller; the strategies do not know each other. State: an order is Draft, then Paid, then Shipped; the current state object decides what Cancel() does (allowed in Draft, refused after Shipped) and also switches the order to the next state. If the object changes its own behaviour by transitions, it is State.

Event subscriptions keep the subscriber alive, so a short-lived object that subscribes to a long-lived publisher and never unsubscribes is never collected.

The publisher's event holds a delegate that points to the subscriber. A singleton service that raises an event and a page or view model that subscribes each time it opens will grow: after 1,000 openings there are 1,000 live objects, each also being called on every event. Fix it by unsubscribing (-=) in Dispose, using weak events, or avoid event-based design for long-lived publishers.

A mediator centralises how objects talk, and the downside is that the logic can hide inside handlers that nobody calls directly, so the flow is hard to follow.

With a mediator, Send(new CreateOrder()) reaches a handler you must search for; "find all references" does not show who triggers what. Pipelines and behaviours add more hidden steps. The extra layer also adds a little runtime cost, and the popular library MediatR became commercial for new versions. For small apps, calling a service method is simpler. A mediator is useful when many features share cross-cutting behaviour such as validation and logging.

code.title: A logging and timing decorator that rethrows with throw;

followUps:
The caching one goes outside, so a cache hit is answered before anything else runs.

Order from the caller inward: cache, then logging, then the database. A hit skips the log and the query; the log then shows only real database calls and their time, which is what you want to measure. If logging were outside, it would log every call including hits, which is also a valid choice when you want to see traffic. Decide what each layer should see, and write the registration order down, because the result changes with the order.

Because throw ex; resets the stack trace to the line where you rethrew, and you lose the place where the error began. throw; keeps it.

catch (Exception e)
{
log.LogError(e, "failed");
throw;        // original stack trace kept
}

With throw ex; the trace of an error deep in the repository would start at your logging decorator, so the log points at the wrong line. To add context, wrap it: throw new RepoException("order " + id, e); so the inner exception is kept.

Use a generated or dynamic proxy, or the decorator support of a library, so the cross-cutting code is written once.

  • DispatchProxy (built in): DispatchProxy.Create<T, LoggingProxy>() intercepts every method of an interface using reflection. Simple, a bit slow.
  • Castle DynamicProxy or similar: more powerful interceptors.
  • Source generators that write the wrappers at build time: fast and AOT friendly.
  • Mediator pipeline behaviours if calls go through handlers, so there is only one place for logging.

For a few interfaces, hand-written decorators are clearer and cheaper to debug.

code.title: Building the chain backwards, and an order mistake that skips a check

followUps:
Write integration tests that call the real pipeline and check the observable result, such as the status code and the headers, for the cases where order matters.

With WebApplicationFactory: an anonymous request to a protected endpoint returns 401; a request from a disallowed origin gets no CORS header; a request with a valid token gets 200; an exception returns Problem Details and not the developer page. If someone moves UseAuthorization above UseAuthentication, the second test fails. These tests read like a specification of the order, and a unit test of each middleware cannot catch this kind of bug.

Short-circuiting in code is a middleware that writes the response and returns without awaiting next.

app.Use(async (ctx, next) =>
{
if (ctx.Request.Path == "/maintenance")
{
ctx.Response.StatusCode = 503;
await ctx.Response.WriteAsync("Back soon");
return;                      // pipeline stops here
}
await next(ctx);
});

Everything registered after it does not run for that request. Middleware before it still gets control back and can add headers or log the 503.

Put it very early, near the top, but after the exception handler, so that every later log line and every error response has the id.

The middleware reads X-Correlation-Id from the request or creates a new GUID, puts it in the response header, and opens a logging scope with it:

using (log.BeginScope(new Dictionary<string, object> { ["CorrelationId"] = id }))
await next(ctx);

If it were after authentication or routing, failures that short-circuit before it would be logged without an id. Also pass the id on to outgoing HTTP calls. With OpenTelemetry the W3C traceparent header does this job.

code.title: The N+1 query anti-pattern, counted

followUps:
Look at the SQL the application actually sends: many near-identical queries for one request is the sign.

  • Application Insights or OpenTelemetry traces: one request with 200 dependency spans of the same SQL text.
  • EF Core logging: enable LogTo or the SQL log category in a test and count the commands.
  • Database tools: query store, pg_stat_statements or Profiler, sorted by call count.
  • Tests: assert the number of queries for a key endpoint.

Fix with Include, a projection with Select, or one batched query.

Rarely, and only at a narrow place that has to find services at run time, like a factory or plug-in lookup, or inside middleware where constructor injection is not available.

An example is a background service that must create a scope for each message: it takes IServiceScopeFactory in its constructor and calls CreateScope(). That is still a form of service location, but it is explicit and small. What is not acceptable is calling GetService across business classes, because it hides dependencies and breaks tests.

A distributed monolith is a set of services that must be deployed and changed together, so you have all the cost of microservices and none of the independence.

Tests to apply: Can one service be released alone? Do changes to one regularly need changes in three others? Do services share a database or call each other synchronously in long chains? Does one failure bring down the rest? If the answers are no, yes, yes and yes, it is a distributed monolith. Real microservices own their data, communicate through stable contracts or events, and fail separately.

code.title: Why a repository returning IQueryable leaks, and a projection that fixes it

followUps:
You test the real code against a real database, and mock only the things outside your control.

Code that uses DbContext directly is best tested as an integration test with SQL Server or PostgreSQL in a Testcontainers container, or SQLite in memory for simple cases. Keep business rules in plain classes with no EF types (a pricing function takes numbers and returns numbers), and unit test those without a database. Mocking DbSet is fragile and does not run your queries, so it proves little.

The specification pattern puts a query condition in its own small reusable object, so that "active customers in Germany" is named once and used in many places.

public class ActiveInCountry(string country)
{
public Expression<Func<Customer, bool>> Criteria =>
c => c.IsActive && c.Country == country;
}
var list = await db.Customers.Where(new ActiveInCountry("DE").Criteria).ToListAsync();

It must be an Expression, not a Func, so EF Core can translate it to SQL. It is useful for rules reused in several queries; for a single query, a plain Where is clearer.

Returning IQueryable lets callers keep adding filters, which spreads query logic everywhere and makes the repository's behaviour unpredictable.

The query is still open, so it executes late, maybe after the DbContext is disposed, causing an error. The caller can add a Where that cannot be translated to SQL and fail at run time, or call ToList() on a huge table. Costs are no longer under the repository's control. Return a finished List or a page of results, or take a specification as input.

code.title: A transactional outbox: save the event with the data, publish afterwards

followUps:
Because it needs a coordinator that locks resources in every service until all agree, and it fails badly when a service or the network is down.

Two-phase commit asks every participant to "prepare", then to "commit". While waiting, locks are held, so one slow service blocks all. If the coordinator dies between the phases, participants are stuck. Many cloud brokers and databases do not support it, and it ties the services' availability together. The usual replacement is the saga with compensating steps plus the outbox, which accept short periods of inconsistency.

In orchestration one central component tells each service what to do next; in choreography services react to each other's events with no central controller.

  • Orchestration: an order saga calls payment, then stock, then shipping, and sends the undo commands on failure. The flow is easy to see and change in one place, but the orchestrator is a dependency.
  • Choreography: payment publishes PaymentTaken, stock listens and publishes StockReserved. Services stay loosely coupled, but the full flow is hard to see and debug.

For long flows with several steps, I prefer orchestration (Durable Functions or a saga library).

A cache stampede is when a popular cache entry expires and hundreds of requests all miss at once and all rebuild it, hitting the database together.

Prevent it with: a lock or "single flight" so only one caller rebuilds while the others wait (HybridCache does this); a random extra time on expiry so keys do not all expire together; refreshing before expiry in the background; or serving the stale value briefly while one request refreshes it. Example: 500 requests a second on a key that takes 2 seconds to rebuild means 1,000 database hits without protection and 1 with it.

The app sees the proxy's address and the wrong scheme instead of the real client's, so redirects, links and logs are wrong.

Behind a load balancer or reverse proxy, TLS usually ends at the proxy and Kestrel receives plain HTTP. Without the forwarded headers middleware, Request.Scheme is http, so a redirect to HTTPS loops or authentication callbacks (OpenID Connect) use http:// redirect URIs that the identity provider rejects. Client IP addresses are the proxy's, which breaks rate limiting. Fix: app.UseForwardedHeaders() with XForwardedFor | XForwardedProto and trust only your proxy's address.

In-process hosting runs your app inside the IIS worker process, and out-of-process runs it as a separate Kestrel process that IIS forwards requests to.

In-process (the default for ASP.NET Core on IIS) is faster because there is no network hop between two processes. Out-of-process is slower but keeps your app separate from the IIS worker, so a crash or a memory problem does not touch it, and the app behaves like it does on Linux. In both cases the ASP.NET Core Module does the hosting work, and the application pool should be set to "No Managed Code".

You let the platform drain the old instance: stop sending it new requests, wait for running ones to finish, then stop it.

  • Handle SIGTERM: ASP.NET Core stops accepting connections and finishes in-flight requests up to ShutdownTimeout.
  • Use readiness probes, so the load balancer stops sending traffic when shutdown starts.
  • In Kubernetes or Azure, use rolling updates or deployment slots and set the grace period at least as long as the longest request.
  • Long jobs should go to a queue and not be tied to a request.

Because a constraint only decides whether a route matches the URL; it does not give the caller a helpful error and does not check business meaning.

A route /{id:int} makes /orders/abc return 404, because no route matches, not 400 with a message. It also cannot say "id must be positive" or "the order must exist". Use constraints to choose between routes (for example {id:guid} and {slug}), and validate the values in the handler or a filter, returning 400 with Problem Details.

ASP.NET Core throws an AmbiguousMatchException at request time when two endpoints match with the same priority, so you get a 500 and not a quiet choice.

Routing scores matches: a literal segment beats a parameter, and a parameter with a constraint beats one without. So /orders/latest wins over /orders/{id}. If scores are equal, such as two /orders/{id} routes with the same verb, you get the exception. Fix by changing the template, adding a constraint, or setting an explicit order.

Give the type a static TryParse method (or implement IParsable<T>), and minimal APIs will bind it from a route or query string by themselves.

public record Range(int From, int To)
{
public static bool TryParse(string? s, out Range? r)
{
var p = s?.Split('-');
r = null;
if (p is { Length: 2 } && int.TryParse(p[0], out var a) && int.TryParse(p[1], out var b)) r = new(a, b);
return r is not null;
}
}
app.MapGet("/items", (Range range) => ...);   // /items?range=5-10

For controllers, use [FromQuery] with a model binder or a type converter. For many fields use [AsParameters] to bind a whole class.

code.title: Edge validation collects every error; the domain still guards its rules

followUps:
Use 400 when the request is malformed and 422 when it is well-formed but fails a rule; both are accepted, so pick one and be consistent.

ASP.NET Core's built-in validation returns 400 with ValidationProblemDetails, which is what most clients expect and what [ApiController] does. Some teams use 422 for semantic errors such as "end date before start date" to tell them apart from broken JSON. The important point is a single documented rule and a single error shape, so that the front end handles it in one place.

Check it inside the service that saves the data, and back it with a unique index in the database; the index is the real guard.

A pre-check (AnyAsync(u => u.Email == email)) gives a friendly message but has a race: two requests can both pass it. The unique index stops the second one, and the code catches the duplicate-key error and turns it into a 409 Conflict or a validation error for the Email field. Do not put this in a data annotation, because it needs the database and is async.

Collect all errors in a dictionary (field to messages) and return them in one ValidationProblem instead of stopping at the first.

var errors = new Dictionary<string, string[]>();
if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(dto.Email)) errors["Email"] = ["required"];
if (dto.Quantity < 1) errors["Quantity"] = ["must be at least 1"];
return errors.Count > 0 ? Results.ValidationProblem(errors) : Results.Ok();

Data annotations and FluentValidation already collect every failure in a run. The user can then fix all fields in one go instead of one error per attempt.

code.title: System.Text.Json defaults: camelCase, nulls and case-insensitive reading

followUps:
Use Newtonsoft.Json when you depend on a feature System.Text.Json does not offer, or when old code relies on its exact behaviour.

Examples: very flexible custom converters, JObject / JToken style editing, JsonPath queries, some old settings for reference loops and polymorphism, and many older libraries (for example Json Patch in MVC) that still use it. System.Text.Json is faster and allocates less, and it now supports most needs, so for new code I start there and add Newtonsoft only for a proven gap.

Mark the base class with [JsonPolymorphic] and list each derived type with [JsonDerivedType] (.NET 7 and later). A type discriminator is written into the JSON.

[JsonPolymorphic(TypeDiscriminatorPropertyName = "kind")]
[JsonDerivedType(typeof(Circle), "circle")]
[JsonDerivedType(typeof(Square), "square")]
public abstract class Shape { }

Without it, serializing a List<Shape> writes only the properties of the base class, and deserializing cannot know which class to create. Only list types you trust, which also protects against type confusion attacks.

Because by default System.Text.Json finds properties at run time with reflection, which the trimmer and Native AOT cannot analyse, so the app breaks or fails to start.

A source generator writes the serialization code at build time for the types you list:

[JsonSerializable(typeof(Order))]
partial class AppJson : JsonSerializerContext { }
JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, AppJson.Default.Order);

Result: no reflection, faster start-up, lower memory, and AOT works. In ASP.NET Core you register the context through ConfigureHttpJsonOptions.

code.title: Generations, finalizers and Dispose: what the GC really does

followUps:
Because an object with a finalizer survives one extra garbage collection and then needs a separate thread to run the finalizer, while Dispose runs immediately in your code.

The GC cannot free a finalizable object when it first finds it dead: it moves it to a queue, runs the finalizer later on the finalizer thread, and frees the memory only at the next collection, often after it has been promoted to an older generation. Resources stay held for that whole time. So implement IDisposable, and call GC.SuppressFinalize(this) in it so the finalizer is skipped when you did the cleanup. Use a finalizer only as a safety net.

In a small container, Workstation GC is usually right, and Server GC with concurrent collection needs more memory and cores to pay off.

Server GC uses one heap and one thread per core, which gives higher throughput on big machines but uses more memory. With 1 CPU and 512 MB it does not help and may waste memory; .NET picks Workstation GC in that case unless you force it. Set limits properly in the container (DOTNET_GCHeapHardLimit or let it read the cgroup limit), and measure with real load. DOTNET_gcServer=1 is worth testing for a busy API with several cores.

Almost never in production code, because the GC knows more than you do about when to run, and forcing a full collection pauses the app.

Valid cases: a benchmark or test that needs a clean start; right after a rare, huge, one-off operation (a big import) where you know memory is mostly garbage; or in a game between levels. A call to GC.Collect() to "fix" a leak only hides it. If memory grows, find what is holding references with a dump (dotnet-gcdump, dotnet-dump) instead.

Because the JIT can see the running program and optimise for what it really does, while an ahead-of-time compiler must guess.

The JIT knows the exact CPU (so it can use the newest vector instructions), which branches are hot, and which concrete type sits behind an interface call (dynamic PGO), and can inline across assemblies. Native AOT compiles once, for a generic CPU, without that knowledge. Native AOT wins at start-up and memory; JIT usually wins at long-running peak throughput. Choose AOT for functions and short-lived tools, and JIT for a busy service that runs for days.

Source generators and compile-time code replace it: the code that reflection used to find at run time is written at build time.

  • JSON: JsonSerializerContext source generation.
  • Logging: [LoggerMessage] generated methods.
  • Configuration binding and minimal API parameter binding have generators (the Request Delegate Generator).
  • DI and mapping: explicit registrations and mapping libraries that generate code, not scan assemblies.

The build then shows trim and AOT warnings (IL2026, IL3050) where something still needs reflection.

Attack the parts of start-up you control, in this order: plan, package, then code.

  1. Use a plan with pre-warmed or always-ready instances (Premium or Flex Consumption).
  2. Publish ReadyToRun, which does part of the JIT work at build time, and use the isolated worker with a small dependency list.
  3. Do no heavy work in Program.cs: no big downloads or large object graphs; initialise lazily.
  4. Keep the package small and run it from the package file.

Measure cold start in Application Insights before and after each change.

code.title: A token-bucket rate limiter returning 429

followUps:
Output caching stores the server's response and sends it to many users; response caching only sets headers so that browsers and proxies may cache it. HybridCache is not for responses at all: it caches data your code computes.

  • Output caching (.NET 7+): the server keeps the response, can vary by query or header, can evict by tag, and works even if the client sends no cache headers.
  • Response caching: follows the HTTP caching rules, honours client Cache-Control, rarely used for APIs.
  • HybridCache: a two-level cache (memory plus Redis) for values in your services.

You keep the counters in a shared store, because the built-in limiter keeps its counters in each instance's memory.

With ten instances behind a load balancer, a limit of 100 per minute per user would really allow about 1,000. Options: apply the limit at the gateway (Azure API Management, YARP, Front Door) that sees all traffic; or store counters in Redis with an atomic increment and expiry; or use a library with a Redis backend. For rough protection, divide the limit by the number of instances and accept the approximation.

It should wait and try again later, respecting the Retry-After header if there is one, and not retry at once.

429 means "too many requests", so retrying immediately only makes it worse. The client should wait the number of seconds in Retry-After, or use exponential backoff with jitter (1s, 2s, 4s plus a random part), limit the number of retries, and slow its own request rate. The API should send Retry-After and a Problem Details body saying which limit was hit.

code.title: A trace id that follows a request through three layers

followUps:
You copy the trace context into the message's properties when you send, and restore it as the parent when you receive.

The W3C traceparent value (trace id, span id, flags) goes in a header of the message, such as Service Bus ApplicationProperties. The consumer reads it and starts its span as a child of that context. Azure SDK clients and MassTransit do this for you when OpenTelemetry is on. The consumer span is usually "linked" to the producer, because processing may happen much later and should not make one very long trace.

Sampling means recording only a fraction of the traces, to control cost and volume. The price is that you may not have the trace for a particular failed request.

With 10 percent sampling, one rare error has only a 1 in 10 chance of being recorded. Head sampling decides at the start of the request; tail sampling decides after it ends, so it can keep all errors and slow requests and only a sample of the fast, successful ones. Always keep metrics and logs unsampled: counters like "errors per minute" stay accurate.

The four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors and saturation.

  • Latency: the 95th or 99th percentile of response time, not the average; failed requests are measured separately.
  • Traffic: requests per second.
  • Errors: rate of 5xx responses, and of failed dependencies.
  • Saturation: how full the resources are: CPU, memory, thread-pool queue length, database connections.

Alert on symptoms users feel (error rate, latency), and use the saturation graphs to find the cause. Page people only for what needs action now.

code.title: Span<T> slices without copying; the cost of Substring

followUps:
Because a span may point into the stack, and a class lives on the heap and can outlive the method that created the stack frame, leaving a pointer to dead memory.

Span is a ref struct: the compiler only lets it live on the stack. So it cannot be a field of a class, be boxed, be captured by a lambda, or be used across an await (the method's state moves to the heap). When you need to store a slice or use it in async code, use Memory<T>, which is a normal struct that can live on the heap and gives you a span with .Span when you need it.

The array stays rented and is never reused, so the pool must create new arrays, and the allocations you wanted to avoid come back.

With ArrayPool<T>.Shared.Rent(1024) you must call Return when done, usually in finally. A forgotten return is not a leak in the classic sense (the GC will free it), but it makes the pool useless and moves cost to the GC. The opposite mistake is worse: using the array after returning it, or returning it twice, because another caller may now own it. Also remember the rented array can be larger than the size you asked for.

You measure it, with BenchmarkDotNet and its memory diagnoser, or with a quick allocation counter before and after.

BenchmarkDotNet reports bytes allocated per operation and the Gen 0 / 1 / 2 collections, for the old and new code side by side: for example "Substring: 40 B per call, span: 0 B". For a quick check, GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() before and after a loop works. In production, watch the allocation rate and GC count in dotnet-counters. Always check that the change makes a difference in time, not only in bytes.

code.title: Thread pool starvation: blocking waits versus real asynchrony

followUps:
Because the pool adds a thread only slowly, about one or two per second once its minimum is used up, to avoid creating hundreds of threads that fight for the CPU.

The minimum threads are created at once, then the pool waits half a second or more before adding another, to see whether queued work finishes by itself. When 500 requests suddenly block, the queue grows much faster than the pool, so latency climbs to many seconds. Raising SetMinThreads is a short-term patch; removing the blocking calls is the cure.

Because ASP.NET Core has no synchronization context, so the continuation after await does not have to return to one specific thread that is blocked.

Classic ASP.NET had a context that allowed only one thread at a time per request. .Result blocked that thread while the awaited task wanted to continue on the same one: a deadlock.
