In ASP.NET Core any pool thread can finish the work, so there is no deadlock. But the blocked thread is still wasted, and many of them cause starvation, as described above. So "does not deadlock" does not mean "is fine".

No. Task.Run only moves the blocking to another pool thread, so the pool still loses a thread and you pay extra scheduling cost.

In a web API the request already runs on a pool thread. await Task.Run(() => BlockingCall()) still holds one pool thread for the whole wait. The real fix is a truly asynchronous API (ReadAsync, HttpClient.GetAsync, async database calls) all the way up the call chain. If a library only has blocking calls, isolate it with a limited number of dedicated threads or a separate worker.

Because an unloadable load context can only be freed when nothing in the process still points into it, and a single stray reference keeps all its assemblies alive.

Common holders: a static field or cache in the host that stores an object from the plug-in; a running thread or timer started by the plug-in; an event handler registered on a host object; a thread-local; and a pinned handle. Unloading is cooperative: you call Unload(), drop your references, and the GC frees it. You can test with a WeakReference to the context in a loop of GC.Collect() calls and see if it is cleared; tools like dotnet-gcroot (in dotnet-dump) show the path that holds it.

It means the same type was loaded twice, from two different load contexts, and the runtime treats them as two different types.

A type's identity is its name plus the assembly load context that loaded it. A plug-in that ships its own copy of a shared contract assembly gets a second copy of IPlugin, so casting the plug-in's object to the host's IPlugin fails with the message "Unable to cast object of type 'X' to type 'X'". The fix is to make the shared contract load only once, from the host's context, for example by resolving it in the plug-in context to the default context.

deps.json lists the exact assemblies and native libraries your app needs; runtimeconfig.json says which runtime to use and its settings.

  • MyApp.deps.json: every package and project dependency with version and file path, so the host knows what to load.
  • MyApp.runtimeconfig.json: the target framework and minimum version (Microsoft.NETCore.App 10.0.0), the roll-forward rule, and settings such as server GC.

Both are generated at build time and sit next to the .dll. If you copy only the dll to a server, the app will not start.

code.title: Modern C# in one file: record, pattern matching, switch expression, primary constructor

followUps:
A record gives you value-based equality, a readable ToString, with expressions and a deconstructor, with one line of code.

For record Point(int X, int Y): two points with the same X and Y are equal (a class compares references); ToString() prints Point { X = 1, Y = 2 }; var moved = p with { X = 5 }; copies with one change; var (x, y) = p; deconstructs. Positional properties are init-only, so records suit DTOs, messages and value objects. EF entities are normally still plain classes, because they are tracked by identity.

They check that you do not use a possibly-null value without a test, but only at compile time and only as warnings.

The compiler tracks a "maybe null" or "not null" state for each reference and warns on name.Length when name may be null. Nothing is added at run time: a null can still get in through reflection, JSON, or code compiled without the feature. So they remove most NullReferenceExceptions but do not guarantee none. Turn on <Nullable>enable</Nullable> and treat warnings as errors in new projects.

Not officially. C# 14 needs the .NET 10 SDK and runtime features, and .NET Framework is a frozen target.

The compiler (SDK) can build a .NET Framework project with a newer language version by setting <LangVersion>, and many features that are compiler-only work (for example pattern matching, file-scoped namespaces). Features that need runtime support, such as default interface methods, Span improvements, or new library types, do not. Microsoft does not support this combination, so use it carefully or move to modern .NET.

The token fires when the client disconnects or aborts the request, or when the server is shutting down.

It is HttpContext.RequestAborted. In a minimal API or controller, add a CancellationToken ct parameter and it is bound to this token. Pass it down to ToListAsync(ct) and HttpClient.GetAsync(url, ct) so that expensive work stops when the user closes the browser tab. Catch OperationCanceledException only to clean up; ASP.NET Core does not log it as an error.

TypedResults return a concrete result type such as Ok<Order>, while Results return a plain IResult.

With the typed version the compiler knows all possible outcomes, Results<Ok<Order>, NotFound>, so OpenAPI is produced automatically and unit tests can check the type. Use TypedResults.Ok(order) and TypedResults.NotFound() in new code.

A record class is a reference type stored on the heap; a record struct is a value type copied on assignment.

record class (just record) allows null, is passed by reference, and its properties are init-only by default. record struct is copied, cannot be null, and its properties are mutable unless you write readonly record struct. Use a readonly record struct for small values such as Money(decimal Amount, string Currency) in hot code; use a record class for larger messages and DTOs.

Replace the colons with double underscores: Payments:Stripe:Key becomes Payments__Stripe__Key.

The configuration system treats __ as the section separator because colons are not allowed in environment variable names on some platforms. Array items use their index: Cors__Origins__0. In Azure App Service the settings page also accepts the double underscore form, and for connection strings the prefixes SQLCONNSTR_ and similar are added by the platform.

Because a typed client is created through IHttpClientFactory with a short lifetime, and holding it in a singleton keeps one handler for ever, which defeats the DNS refresh.

The factory recycles the underlying handlers about every two minutes so that DNS changes are noticed. A singleton that stores the client keeps the first connection forever. Either register the client as transient (the default) and let each consumer receive it, or if a singleton needs it, inject IHttpClientFactory and call CreateClient when needed.

Blazor is better when the team is made of C# developers who want one language and one code base for server and browser, and when the app is an internal or line-of-business tool.

It lets you share models and validation with the back end, and avoids a second toolchain (npm, bundlers). It is weaker where you need a huge component ecosystem, strict first-load size for public sites, a team already strong in React or Angular, or hiring from the JavaScript market. For a public content site, server rendering with Razor or a JS framework may suit better.

HybridCache adds a second level and protection against many callers rebuilding the same entry at once, which IDistributedCache does not do.

IDistributedCache only stores and returns bytes: you write the serialization, the miss handling and the locking yourself. HybridCache gives one call, GetOrCreateAsync(key, factory), with an in-memory first level, a distributed second level, serialization, stampede protection and tags. Fewer code lines and fewer database hits; it was released with .NET 9 and runs on .NET 8 through a package.

Named query filters (EF Core 10) let you define several global query filters on one entity and switch each one off by name, instead of an all-or-nothing switch.

Before, an entity had one filter (for example soft delete and tenant together) and IgnoreQueryFilters() turned all of them off. Now you give each filter a name, such as "SoftDelete" and "Tenant", and a query can ignore only one: IgnoreQueryFilters(["SoftDelete"]). This is useful for an admin screen that must see deleted rows but must still respect the tenant.

Answer honestly: name what you shipped, what you tried in a side project, and what you only read about.

A good reply is: "In production I have used keyed services and minimal APIs for two years. I tried HybridCache in a test service and measured fewer database calls. Native AOT I have read about, but not shipped." Interviewers value truth and the reasons for a choice far more than a list of features. Prepare one or two real examples with numbers.

code.title: LINQ deferred execution and a left join

followUps:
Use a group join and then DefaultIfEmpty(), so that people without orders still appear once.

var q = from p in people
join o in orders on p.Id equals o.PersonId into g
from o in g.DefaultIfEmpty()
select new { p.Name, Item = o?.Item };

Ana with one order gives one row; Ben with no orders gives one row with Item = null. With EF Core, in .NET 10 there is also a LeftJoin method that does this directly. If the entities have a navigation property, Select(p => new { p.Name, Orders = p.Orders }) is simpler.

SelectMany flattens: for each item it takes a list and joins all the lists into one sequence.

Example: customers with orders [Ana: 2 orders, Ben: 0, Cy: 3]. customers.Select(c => c.Orders) gives 3 lists, but customers.SelectMany(c => c.Orders) gives one sequence of 5 orders. It is the LINQ form of a nested loop and is also what two from lines in query syntax become. In EF Core it becomes a join.

A method with yield return is turned by the compiler into a small state machine that remembers where it stopped, and it runs only as far as the consumer asks.

Calling the method runs none of its code. Each MoveNext() (a foreach step) runs the body until the next yield return, hands back that value and pauses with its local variables kept. So Take(3) on an endless generator stops after three values. Beware: a bug or exception inside the method appears when you enumerate, not when you call it, and each enumeration starts again from the top.

code.title: Open/closed and dependency inversion: add a rule without editing the calculator

followUps:
Dependency inversion is the design rule; dependency injection is the technique that supplies the object.

The rule: your business code should depend on an interface that it owns, and the infrastructure (SQL, mail) should implement that interface, so the dependency points toward the business code. Injection: a container or the composition root passes in the implementation. You can follow the rule with plain constructor parameters and no container at all, and you can use a container while still depending on concrete classes everywhere.

A common case is splitting every small class behind an interface and a factory "for single responsibility" until one simple feature spans eight files.

Example: a form with one validation rule became IValidator, ValidatorBase, ValidatorFactory and a registry. Nobody could follow the flow, and nothing ever had a second implementation. The cost of indirection, in reading time and debugging, was greater than the benefit. Apply the principle when you can name the change it protects against; if a class has one reason to change and one implementation, leave it simple.

Small, focused interfaces mean a test double only has to implement the few methods the code under test uses.

If IOrderService has 25 methods and a handler calls two, a fake must still implement all 25, or you use a mocking library to hide this. With IOrderReader (2 methods) and IOrderWriter the fake is five lines. It also shows in the constructor what a class does: a class that takes only a reader cannot write. Large interfaces also cause changes in unrelated tests when a method is added.

code.title: Characterisation test and a seam around DateTime.Now

followUps:
Put each of them behind a small interface (a seam), so a test can supply a fake, and keep the old behaviour unchanged.

public class ReportService(TimeProvider clock, IOrderStore store)
{
public bool IsOverdue(Order o) => o.Due < clock.GetUtcNow();
}

For DateTime.Now use TimeProvider (.NET 8). For a static database helper, create an interface with the same method, make the old static class call a real implementation, and pass the interface in. If you cannot change the call sites yet, a first step is a wrapper that forwards to the static code, so tests replace the wrapper.

Tie refactoring to features and bugs, and show the numbers, so it is not a separate request.

  • Refactor the area you are about to change, as part of that ticket ("clean as you go").
  • Show cost: how many days the last three changes in that module took, and how many bugs came from it.
  • Offer small, visible steps of one or two days with a clear result, not a "rewrite quarter".
  • Keep a small, regular share of time (for example 10 to 20 percent) for tech debt.

Business people respond to speed and risk, not to code cleanliness.

A rewrite is right only when the old system cannot be changed safely and keeping it costs more than starting again, and even then I prefer to replace it piece by piece.

Reasons that justify it: the platform is unsupported and cannot run, nobody understands it and there are no tests, the architecture blocks every needed feature, or the business logic is small and well specified. Big-bang rewrites often run late and lose hidden behaviour. The safer way is the strangler pattern: route one feature at a time to new code behind a proxy, until the old one is empty.

Turn it on one project at a time, and fix warnings in small groups, so that you never have thousands at once.

  1. Add <Nullable>enable</Nullable> to one new or small project first.
  2. In older files use #nullable enable per file, or set annotations first, then warnings.
  3. Fix files you touch anyway; mark real nulls with ?.
  4. Turn the nullable warnings into errors in CI, per project, once a project is clean.

Do not silence warnings with ! unless you know the value is not null.

I would listen to the reasons, try it on a real example together, and agree a team rule; a standard should not depend on who argues loudest.

Primary constructors are fine for simple dependency injection, but parameters captured as mutable state can surprise people, and some find them less readable. A good result is a written convention such as "use for DI services, not for entities", enforced with an .editorconfig rule so it is not a taste argument in every review. Respect the senior's experience, and revisit the rule after a few months.

Yes, but only with a plan to move on time, because it has a shorter support period and only when it gives something the product needs.

STS now gets 24 months of support, which is enough for a team that deploys often and upgrades every year. I would choose it for a new service with automated tests and containers, where an upgrade is a small change. I would not use it for software that customers install, for regulated systems with slow validation, or in a team that finds upgrades hard. Whichever line, schedule the upgrade in the roadmap from the first day.
